State Behaviors

State Behaviors provide a deterministic, centralized mechanism for committing and exposing pipeline results as authoritative state snapshots. State behaviors finalize pipeline outcomes, normalize state transitions, and emit immutable snapshots that represent the completed result of pipeline execution.

State Contract Summary

  • State behaviors must not derive or transform candidate values
  • State behaviors must not control pipeline execution or admission
  • State behaviors must emit exactly one authoritative state snapshot per execution
  • State behaviors must not mutate previously emitted snapshots
  • Core state handling is always executed and cannot be omitted

The State contract guarantees that state commitment is deterministic and isolated. Regardless of how pipeline execution completes—success, suppression, error, stop, reset, or destruction—the State stage finalizes execution by committing a single, canonical state snapshot.

State behaviors do not participate in value derivation, policy evaluation, scheduling, or control flow. Their sole responsibility is to finalize pipeline execution and expose the resulting state in a consistent, observable form.

State Stage

The State Stage is responsible for finalizing and committing pipeline outcomes into the FeatureCell’s authoritative state snapshot. It represents the exclusive execution boundary where resolved values, loading transitions, and error states are atomically applied and emitted as immutable state snapshots.

The State Stage executes after successful pipeline completion, controlled termination, or error finalization. It guarantees that each pipeline execution results in a single, deterministic state emission that reflects the final outcome of that execution.

State behaviors:

  • Operate exclusively on immutable state snapshot shapes
  • Commit finalized values, loading transitions, and error states
  • Emit authoritative state snapshots representing pipeline completion
  • Do not derive new values or influence pipeline control flow
  • Must preserve atomicity and snapshot consistency

Core Pipeline Stage

The State stage is a core pipeline stage and is always present as part of the FeatureCell lifecycle. A core state behavior executes first to guarantee that all pipeline outcomes are committed consistently and emitted as a canonical state snapshot. This behavior cannot be omitted. Optional add-on state behaviors may observe the finalized snapshot but must not alter it.

State behaviors do not resume pipeline execution, re-enter processing stages, or modify committed outcomes. Their responsibility ends once the finalized state snapshot has been emitted to observers.

Updating State

While the State Stage is responsible for committing finalized pipeline outcomes, state updates are initiated through the FeatureCell API. A FeatureCell exposes three distinct mechanisms for submitting state updates into the pipeline: replaceState(), mergeState(), fromStream(), fromDeferred(), fromObservable(), and fromPromise().

Each mechanism enters the pipeline through a different admission path but ultimately resolves, processes, and commits state through the same deterministic pipeline stages.

Execution Guarantees

  • All update mechanisms enter the pipeline through standard admission.
  • All inputs are processed by the Resolve stage before downstream execution.
  • The State stage commits exactly one authoritative state snapshot per execution.
  • Committed state remains immutable once emitted.

The difference between these mechanisms lies in how candidate state is produced: replaceState() forwards a resolved value directly, mergeState() combines it with existing committed state using a Merge behavior, and fromStream() produces repeated candidate updates over time.

Regardless of admission path, state commitment remains centralized and deterministic within the State stage.

Add-on State Emit Callback Behaviors

In addition to core state commitment and snapshot emission, FeatureCells may opt into add-on state emit callback behaviors. These behaviors observe finalized state snapshots after they have been committed and emitted and may perform supplemental, observational handling after emission such as logging, integration hooks, or compatibility callbacks.

State emit callbacks do not participate in state derivation, do not influence pipeline control flow, and do not alter committed state. Their sole responsibility is to observe immutable state snapshots that have already been finalized by the State stage.

Emit-state callbacks exist solely for convenience and backward compatibility with imperative or callback-oriented codebases. The primary and recommended mechanisms for observing state are the reactive .state$ observable or the synchronous .state getter (exposed as a signal in /Angular). Emit-state callbacks are strictly observational and should not be used for core application logic.

Fluent emitStates() API

A FeatureCell may declare multiple state emit callbacks using the fluent .emitStates() API. This API accepts an ordered array of callbacks that are executed sequentially for each finalized state snapshot. Callback registration occurs during FeatureCell initialization.

Emit-state callbacks are strictly observational. They do not return values, do not modify the snapshot, and always yield VAULT_NOOP. An empty emitStates array is ignored and has no effect on pipeline execution.

Engineer-Supplied State Emit Callbacks

State emit callbacks are supplied by engineers during FeatureCell initialization and execute exclusively after the authoritative state snapshot has been committed. Each callback receives the immutable state snapshot representing pipeline completion.

Callbacks must not throw, must not mutate state, and must not attempt to resume or interrupt pipeline execution. Any errors raised by callbacks are isolated and do not affect state finalization or downstream observers.

Note

Although multiple emit-state callbacks may be composed, callback logic should remain narrowly scoped and observational. These callbacks are best suited for transitional integrations, diagnostics, or legacy interoperability rather than primary state consumption.
